overview: Systems come in off the Pacific one after another this week, reaching the Coast Mountains and Cascades first. The Northeast gets a cold front Monday and a larger storm around Thanksgiving. The Rockies stay mostly dry until a northwest flow late Thursday.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Rain and snow come in waves off the Pacific all week. Cypress Mountain is the strongest, with a peak of 21 inches Thursday. Whistler's peak of 21 inches comes Tuesday, and snow levels stay low enough for both mountains to hold snow. Expect rain at lower elevations on several days.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: A stronger front arrives Tuesday into Wednesday, bringing snow to the mountains and heavy rain to the lowlands. Crystal Mountain's peak of 35 inches comes Thursday, and Mt. Baker follows with 26 inches. Winds are gusty, and snow levels hover near 3000 to 3500 feet during the storm.

regions.title: Northeast
regions.text: A sharp cold front brings blustery winds Monday into Tuesday. A larger storm is more likely around Thanksgiving, and the forecasters say precipitation types and amounts are still uncertain. Le Massif and Mont-Sainte-Anne are both forecast for about 25 inches Friday, with flurries and strong winds lingering into the weekend.

regions.title: Kootenays
regions.text: Light flurries and mixed rain and snow dominate, with the snow mostly at higher elevations. Revelstoke's biggest day is Thursday, at 5 inches, and totals stay modest across the region.

regions.title: Northern Rockies
regions.text: Light snow showers come Monday, mostly in the western mountains, with little accumulation. Tuesday and Wednesday turn dry as a ridge builds in. The next system arrives late Thursday with northwest flow, and Grand Targhee's peak of 6 inches comes Friday.

regions.title: Okanagan
regions.text: Mostly flurries and light showers early in the week, then rain showers Thursday and Friday. Big White's best day is Thursday, at 4 inches, and SilverStar and Sun Peaks see little more than that.

ahead.text: The Weather Prediction Center says a wet pattern continues through the holiday weekend for the West Coast, with multiple days of precipitation in the Northwest. Its extended discussion covers only through Sunday, Nov 29.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
